subject: English
description: Common preposition errors — in/on/at, between/among, since/for, beside/besides

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'I have been waiting ___ him for two hours.'

options.option_text: to (verb-targeting form)
for (object of waiting)
at (location preposition)
with (companionship form)

questions.explanation: WAIT FOR somebody/something — standard collocation. 'For' indicates the object you're waiting for. 'Wait at' (a place), 'wait until' (time). Distractor 'wait to' is incorrect with a person object.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The book is divided ___ ten chapters.'

options.option_text: in (used for static interior position)
into (used for division or transformation)
on (used for surface or topic contact)
with (used for instrument or company)

questions.explanation: DIVIDE INTO — used for splitting into parts. 'Divide a cake into 8 pieces.' 'Translate into Hindi.' 'Convert into smaller units.' Distractor 'in' is for static location. Distractors 'on' and 'with' are wrong contexts.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'There was a quarrel ___ the four brothers.'

options.option_text: between (used for exactly two parties)
among (used for three or more groups)
in (locative for static inner space)
with (used for tools or company)

questions.explanation: BETWEEN — for TWO things or distinct individual items ('between you and me'; 'between Delhi and Mumbai'). AMONG — for MORE THAN TWO viewed as a group ('among the four brothers'). Modern usage allows 'between' for individual relationships even with more than two ('disagreements between the five members'), but standard rule favours AMONG for groups.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'She has been working here ___ 2018.'

options.option_text: for (used with durations)
since (used with start points)
from (used with motion away)
in (used with a location)

questions.explanation: SINCE — used with a STARTING POINT in time (since 2018, since Monday, since 9 a.m.). FOR — used with a DURATION (for two years, for a long time). Both go with PERFECT tenses ('have been working'). Distractor 'from' implies movement; 'in 2018' would mark a specific year, not a continuing duration.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'He sat ___ his friend during the lecture.'

options.option_text: besides (meaning 'in addition to')
beside (meaning 'next to')
on (incorrect with a person)
between (needs two parties)

questions.explanation: BESIDE = next to (physical position). 'She sat beside me.' BESIDES = in addition to / apart from. 'Besides English, he speaks French.' Don't confuse the two — common error. Distractor 'on' would mean physically on the friend's lap (not appropriate). 'Between' would need two anchors.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'I will see you ___ Monday morning.'

options.option_text: in (used for years/months)
on (used for days/dates)
at (used for clock times)
by (used for deadlines only)

questions.explanation: ON — for days + dates: ON Monday, ON 15 August, ON my birthday. AT — for clock times: AT 5 pm, AT noon, AT midnight. IN — for months/years/longer periods: IN April, IN 2026, IN the morning. BY — for deadlines: 'finish BY Monday'. 'On Monday morning' is correct because Monday is a day; the 'morning' is a sub-part of that day, so 'on' wins over 'in'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The price has gone up ___ 10%.'

options.option_text: to (used for the final end-point)
by (used for amount of change)
with (used for tools or company)
on (used for surface or topic)

questions.explanation: BY + percentage/amount = quantity of CHANGE. 'Increased BY 10%' = grew by that amount. 'Went up TO ₹500' = the new value is ₹500 (end point). 'Reduced BY half' = halved. 'Increased TO twice' = doubled. Common confusion in financial reporting; 'up by 10%' and 'up to 10%' mean different things.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The government officer was charged ___ accepting bribes from the contractors.

options.option_text: for — typically signals reason or purpose only
with — standard collocation for legal offences
of — pairs with 'accuse' and 'acquit', not 'charge'
by — marks the agent in passive constructions

questions.explanation: 'Charged with' is the fixed legal collocation in both British and Indian legal usage — you charge someone WITH an offence. Option C ('of') is the most tempting distractor because 'accused of' and 'acquit of' both use 'of', but 'charge' uniquely takes 'with'. 'For' signals reason and cannot replace 'with' here.

questions.stem: The renowned scientist was married ___ a celebrated poet for forty years.

options.option_text: with — incorrectly used; 'wed with' is non-standard
by — marks the officiating authority, not the spouse
to — the only correct preposition after 'married'
at — indicates location, not a relational partner

questions.explanation: 'Married to' is the only correct form when naming the spouse; 'to' expresses the relational bond. 'With' is the most common error — candidates confuse it with 'live with' or 'stay with', but 'married with' is non-standard in formal English. 'By' is used only to name the officiating priest or registrar.

questions.stem: After three days of deliberation, the panel finally arrived ___ a unanimous verdict.

options.option_text: at — fixed idiom: 'arrive at' a conclusion or verdict
on — used for surfaces and topics, not conclusions
to — marks direction of movement, not a reasoned endpoint
in — marks location inside something, not a reached result

questions.explanation: 'Arrive at' is the fixed idiomatic collocation when the object is an abstract endpoint such as a decision, verdict, or conclusion. 'To' is the most seductive wrong choice because 'travel to' and 'go to' are familiar, but the idiom for reaching a mental conclusion is specifically 'arrive at', not 'arrive to'. 'On' collocates with topics ('on the matter') but not with reaching a verdict.

questions.stem: The historian attributed the rapid decline of the Mughal Empire ___ administrative inefficiency.

options.option_text: with — used for association or accompaniment, not cause
for — signals reason but does not collocate with 'attribute'
by — marks agent in passive; 'attributed by' needs an agent
to — 'attribute to' is the standard causal collocation

questions.explanation: 'Attribute X to Y' is the fixed collocation: the effect (X) is attributed to its cause or source (Y). 'For' is the chief distractor because it can signal reason in many contexts ('praised for', 'blamed for'), but the verb 'attribute' specifically requires 'to'. 'By' would be correct only if restructured to passive with an agent: 'attributed by historians to…'.

questions.stem: In formal academic writing, a researcher's conclusions must remain independent ___ personal bias.

options.option_text: against — implies active opposition, not freedom from influence
of — 'independent of' is the standard formal collocation
with — implies association, the opposite of independence
from — informal register; 'independent from' is non-standard

questions.explanation: In formal and academic English, 'independent of' is the prescribed collocation — the adjective takes 'of' to mark what is being distanced from. 'From' is a persistent learner error, partly influenced by 'free from'; while 'independent from' appears in casual speech, formal style guides and exam answer keys consistently prefer 'independent of'. 'Against' changes the meaning entirely to confrontation.

questions.stem: The High Court acquitted the defendant ___ all charges after the key witness turned hostile.

options.option_text: of — 'acquit of' is the fixed legal collocation in English
from — a common error; 'acquit from' is not standard in law
with — used with 'charge', the semantically opposite legal verb
for — marks reason or purpose, not legal discharge of liability

questions.explanation: In legal English, one is 'acquitted OF' charges — the preposition 'of' signals separation from the burden of the charge. 'From' is the most common error here: candidates reason by analogy with 'released from' or 'freed from', but both Indian and British courts consistently use 'acquit of'. Note the contrast with the opposite procedure: one is 'charged WITH' but 'acquitted OF'.

questions.stem: All vendors participating in the government tender must comply ___ the specifications outlined in the bid document.

options.option_text: to — a persistent error; 'comply to' is not accepted in formal usage
by — marks agent or instrument, not adherence to a standard
with — 'comply with' is the only correct form in formal English
on — indicates topic or surface, not conformance to regulations

questions.explanation: 'Comply with' is the mandatory collocation in formal, legal, and official English — rules, standards, orders, and specifications are all complied WITH. 'To' is the single most frequent error among test-takers, likely by analogy with 'adhere to' or 'submit to', but 'comply to' is grammatically non-standard and is routinely marked wrong on SSC, IBPS, and RRB papers. 'By' would work only in passive constructions naming the agent.
